query: Which material can be used for superconducting properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high‐entropy alloy (HEA) with an increased fraction of superconducting elements such as Nb and Ta will exhibit superconducting properties when cooled below a critical temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline high‐entropy alloy with a multi‐element composition that does not initially show superconductivity.
generation.intervention: Increase the relative content of known superconducting elements (Nb and Ta) within the HEA composition.
generation.conditions: Cooling to sufficiently low temperatures (in the conventional superconducting regime) where electron–phonon interactions can favor Cooper pair formation.
generation.structural_mediator: An altered electronic density of states and modified phonon spectra resulting from the enhanced Nb/Ta fraction within the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The higher concentration of Nb and Ta improves the electronic states and promotes electron–phonon coupling, which in turn enhances conditions for Cooper pair formation. This adjustment is expected to enable the transition to a superconducting state as evidenced by zero electrical resistance and Meissner effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA will display superconducting behavior, exhibiting zero electrical resistance and magnetic field expulsion below a characteristic critical temperature.
generation.baseline: The original HEA composition with lower Nb/Ta content, which does not show superconductivity under the same experimental conditions.
generation.boundary: The effect is dependent on reaching a threshold level of Nb/Ta content; if the increase is insufficient or if other elements introduce excessive disorder that impedes electron–phonon interactions, the superconducting behavior may not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: The exact Nb/Ta fraction needed, the optimal phase stability, and the precise modification of the electronic and phonon properties required for superconductivity in a complex HEA matrix remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high‐entropy alloy samples: one with a baseline composition and another with an increased Nb/Ta fraction. Subject both sample sets to identical low-temperature environments and measure their electrical resistance and magnetic response as a function of temperature.
measurements: Temperature-dependent electrical resistivity to detect the onset of zero resistance
Magnetic susceptibility to detect the Meissner effect
Critical temperature determination for superconducting transition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA with increased Nb/Ta content does not display a measurable decrease to zero resistance and lacks evidence of the Meissner effect relative to the baseline sample, then the hypothesis that the compositional modification induces superconductivity is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization

decision.trend: Over the past decade, research on high‐entropy and refractory alloys has concentrated on tuning compositions and processing routes to optimize mechanical, thermal, and irradiation‐resistance properties. Several studies have focused on using composition adjustments to achieve superior strength, ductility, and phase stability – for example, by incorporating elements like Nb and Ta, which are well known from conventional superconductors though not originally targeted for superconductivity. Despite these advances, these works have not explicitly probed or optimized the electronic structure for superconducting behavior.
decision.unsolved: How to design and validate an alloy system, particularly within the high‐entropy alloy framework, that not only meets mechanical demands but also reliably exhibits the essential superconducting phenomena (zero electrical resistance and the Meissner effect) remains undemonstrated. In other words, the challenge is to predict and realize the correct electronic densities of states and lattice interactions that favor Cooper pairing.
decision.lever: Increase the fraction of known superconducting elements (e.g., Nb and Ta) within a high‐entropy alloy composition to tailor the electronic density of states and phonon spectra that promote Cooper pair formation
decision.why: This step follows naturally from the trend of compositional tuning in high‐entropy alloys, leveraging elements with well‐established superconducting properties. By systematically varying the Nb/Ta content, researchers can directly target the electronic and lattice parameters critical for superconductivity, thus addressing the open question of which alloy composition can fulfill the superconducting criteria.
